transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

Honestly, I came in because during long sales strategy meetings, I keep getting up even though I know I’m supposed to stay seated. I’ll go refill my water or pace by the printer—just feel like I need to move around.
Outside of feeling restless, do you often have trouble keeping your attention focused on your work tasks?

Yes. In longer strategy meetings, or if I’m reading a client brief, I’ll start out focused, but after a few minutes I realize I’ve been staring at the same slide or paragraph and don’t even know what the last point was.
Did you have similar difficulties with paying attention or sitting still when you were a child in school?

Yes, definitely. It was well before high school. My elementary school teachers would say I was bright, but that I rushed through things, talked out of turn, and forgot my homework. My desk was always full of half-finished papers.
Do these difficulties with staying organized, focused, or restless also affect your daily life at home or in your personal relationships?

Yes. It’s started to affect my work enough that it’s come up in performance reviews, and I worry about how clients see me. There was one complaint from a client that really bothered me—I care a lot about doing good work, and it made me worry I could hurt an account.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient demonstrates pervasive symptoms of both inattention (difficulty sustaining focus on tasks/reading, mind wandering) and hyperactivity/impulsivity (inability to remain seated, restlessness, pacing). Symptoms were present in childhood prior to age 12 (elementary school reports of disorganization, talking out of turn, incomplete work) and cause significant occupational impairment affecting performance reviews and client relationships.
